message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"7b3428af4ad880fda4aa532c0fb83e3f4f598681a75a4490c30566e2589a39f3","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-al-class-d:lineage:60","source_registry_sha256":"ea8231e949706ecda9f2a398d6eaf9ab30e224ac7defb0e6291b764b84ed0d95","units":[{"unit_id":"sec04-u01","module_id":"sec04-m01","objective_ids":["sec04-u01"],"title":{"text":"Good habits from the start","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Good habits on every trip, short or long, are what the manual says make a safe driver.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},{"text":"A set routine before the ignition and when pulling out prevents the most basic mistakes.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F05"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Alex climbs into a car parked at the curb with two friends and wants to head out.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F05"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Alex first adjusts the seat and mirrors, makes sure everyone is seated and buckled, then starts the car and checks over the shoulder and in the mirrors.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F05"]},"result":{"text":"Once traffic is clear, Alex signals, enters the nearest lane and stays there until a lane change is safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a road with no painted lines has no lanes to keep to.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F06"]},"correction":{"text":"A traffic lane is any part of the road wide enough for safe travel, marked or not, and you must keep within one.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Adjust, buckle, start, look, signal, go.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F05"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You drive an automatic. What must be true as you turn the key?","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"The indicator is in park or neutral and your foot is on the brake.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"With an automatic, park or neutral plus the brake comes with the key; with a manual, the clutch is pushed in first.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Habits that keep you safe","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Good habits on every trip.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"A routine before you move.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"This chapter is about the driving task itself, and it starts with habits. The manual describes a safe driver as someone who knows and respects the rules, follows proper procedures, keeps a good attitude and is courteous at all times, using good habits on every trip, whether it is short or long. In this lesson you will build a simple routine: what to do when you get into the car, how to start the engine, how to sit and hold the wheel, how to leave a parallel parking space, and how to keep your place in a lane once you are moving.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Before the ignition","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Adjust seat and mirrors.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Seat passengers; everyone buckles up.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Before you switch on the ignition, set yourself up. Adjust the seat and the mirrors so you can reach the controls and see around you. Make sure passengers are seated so they will not interfere with your driving. Then buckle up, and see that every passenger buckles up too, all before the engine starts. Starting depends on the car. With a manual transmission, push in the clutch before turning the key. With an automatic, have the indicator in park or neutral and press the brake as you turn the key. Getting these steps in order every time becomes a habit.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Posture and grip","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sit upright, both hands on the rim.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},{"text":"Firm grip, not so tight it slows you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Sit upright and hold the outside rim of the steering wheel with both hands. Your grip should be firm enough to control the car, but not so tight that it slows your reflexes. Take a hand off the wheel only to signal or to operate the vehicle, such as a switch or the gear selector, and then put it back. This position gives you the most control in an emergency and keeps your movements smooth. A relaxed but steady grip lets you react quickly instead of fighting the wheel with stiff arms. Keep both hands on the rim whenever you are not signaling or working a control.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pulling out and lane keeping","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Look, wait, signal, enter the nearest lane.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},{"text":"Stay in one lane, marked or not.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"To leave a parallel parking space, look over your shoulder and in the mirrors, wait until the way is clear, signal, and pull into the nearest lane. Stay in that lane until a lane change is safe. Once you are moving, you must keep within a single lane, never weaving between lanes or straddling the lane marking. Remember that a traffic lane is any part of the road wide enough for a vehicle or a line of vehicles to travel safely, and it exists whether or not lines are painted on the road surface. This routine keeps you predictable to the drivers around you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Lanes without lines","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F06","sec04-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"No paint does not mean no lane.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F06","sec04-F05"]},{"text":"Weaving and straddling are never allowed.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F06","sec04-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"A common mistake is to think that lane rules only apply where lines are painted. In fact, a lane exists wherever the road is wide enough for a vehicle or a line of vehicles to travel safely, marked or not. So on a country road without markings, or where paint has worn away, you still keep within a single lane and never weave or straddle. The same goes for pulling out from the curb: you enter the nearest lane and stay there until a lane change is safe, rather than cutting straight across to a far lane. Painted lines help, but they are not what creates a lane.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F06","sec04-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check your starting routine","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Automatic car: what as you turn the key?","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you drive a car with an automatic transmission. What must be true as you turn the key? Decide first, then listen. The answer is that the indicator is in park or neutral and your foot is pressing the brake. With a manual transmission the step is different, because you push in the clutch before turning the key. Either way, the seat, mirrors and seat belts come first, before the ignition, so the whole routine runs: adjust, buckle up, then start the engine the right way for your car. Getting the order right every time is the habit.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Your daily routine","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Adjust, buckle, start correctly.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},{"text":"Look, signal, keep one lane.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, safe driving starts with habits you use every time. Adjust the seat and mirrors, make sure passengers are seated, and have everyone buckle up before the ignition. Start a manual with the clutch in, or an automatic in park or neutral with the brake pressed. Sit upright and grip the outside rim with both hands, firm but not tight. Leave a parallel space by looking, waiting, signaling and entering the nearest lane. Then stay within a single lane, remembering that lanes exist whether or not they are marked.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u02","module_id":"sec04-m02","objective_ids":["sec04-u02"],"title":{"text":"Turns and turn signals","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F10"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Turns are where drivers, pedestrians and cyclists meet, so a clear routine prevents many collisions.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F10","sec04-F11"]},{"text":"Signaling early tells pedestrians and drivers what you plan to do.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Pat is driving on a four-lane highway and needs to turn left at the next cross street.","fact_ids":["sec04-F14","sec04-F08"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Pat moves early to the lane nearest the center line, signals at least one hundred feet before the turn, and keeps both hands on the wheel through it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F14","sec04-F09","sec04-F10"]},"result":{"text":"Pat turns from the inside lane without a wide swing, enters just right of the cross street's center line, and cancels the signal.","fact_ids":["sec04-F14","sec04-F11","sec04-R01"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking hand and arm signals replace signal lights in bright sunlight.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F12"]},"correction":{"text":"Signal lights remain the standard; in daylight you may add hand and arm signals because sunlight can make the light hard to see.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Plan early, signal one hundred feet, cancel after.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-R02"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"How far ahead of a turn should your signal be on, and when does it go off?","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F09"]},"answer":{"text":"At least one hundred feet ahead, kept on until you turn, and switched off once the turn is complete.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F09"]},"rationale":{"text":"The signal tells others your plan early, stays on until the turn, and is cancelled afterward.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F11"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Turning with a plan","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Plan early, signal early.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]},{"text":"Choose the right lane.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"Turning looks simple, but it is one of the busiest moments in driving, because you cross paths with other drivers, pedestrians and cyclists. This lesson builds a turning routine. You will learn to plan each turn early rather than at the last moment, how far ahead to signal and for how long, what to check before and during the turn, and when hand and arm signals help. Then you will see exactly which lane to start from and finish in when turning right or left from a four-lane or divided highway, because lane choice is a favorite test topic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Plan and signal early","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Move to the turn lane well before.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-R02"]},{"text":"Signal at least one hundred feet ahead.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Plan each turn early instead of at the last moment, and move into the proper turn lane well before the turn, once the lane change is safe. Signal at least one hundred feet before turning, and keep the signal on until you actually turn, so both pedestrians and drivers know what you intend to do. Once the turn is complete, switch the signal off. A signal that comes too late gives others no warning, and one left blinking after the turn can mislead drivers who think you are about to turn again. A well-timed signal is a courtesy as well as a rule.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The turning routine","fact_ids":["sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slow down; check front, rear and sides.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Both hands; pedestrians come first.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"As you reach the turn, slow down and check the front, rear and sides for cars and pedestrians. Keep both hands on the wheel during the turn itself, and remember that pedestrians have the right of way over motor vehicles. Finish the turn in the proper lane, then cancel the signal. In daylight you may also add hand and arm signals to your signal lights, because bright sunlight can make a flashing signal hard to see. Those hand signals are an extra, not a substitute, so the signal lights still do the main job. Pedestrians always come first.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Right turns on big roads","fact_ids":["sec04-F13","sec04-F09","sec04-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right lane in, well ahead.","fact_ids":["sec04-F13","sec04-F09","sec04-F11"]},{"text":"Turn tightly into the right lane.","fact_ids":["sec04-F13","sec04-F09","sec04-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"On a four-lane or divided highway, a right turn starts with getting into the right lane well ahead of the turn. Then turn tightly into the right lane of the cross street, rather than swinging out into other lanes. Tight right turns keep you out of the path of traffic in the far lanes of the street you are entering. Combine this with the routine you already know: plan early, signal at least one hundred feet ahead, slow and check all around, keep both hands on the wheel, and cancel the signal when you are done. Tight turns are safer turns.","fact_ids":["sec04-F13","sec04-F09","sec04-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Left turns on big roads","fact_ids":["sec04-F14","sec04-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Use the lane nearest the center line.","fact_ids":["sec04-F14","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"No wide swing; end just right of center.","fact_ids":["sec04-F14","sec04-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"For a left turn from a four-lane or divided highway, move into the lane nearest the center line or divider. Turn from that inside lane without a wide swing, and enter the cross street just to the right of its center line. If signs or pavement markings allow turns from more than one lane, follow them. Left turns cross oncoming traffic, so the early lane change, the early signal and a careful check of pedestrians and other vehicles matter even more than on a right turn. Finish in the proper lane and cancel the signal.","fact_ids":["sec04-F14","sec04-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Right lane versus inside lane","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-R03","sec04-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right turns: right lane to right lane.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-R03","sec04-R02"]},{"text":"Left turns: inside lane, no swing.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-R03","sec04-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is where learners slip. A right turn from a four-lane highway starts in the right lane and ends tightly in the cross street's right lane. A left turn starts from the inside lane, the one nearest the center line, and ends just right of the cross street's center line. Swinging wide on either turn puts you in another driver's path. A second slip is about signals: hand and arm signals may be added in daylight, but they add to the signal lights, never replace them, and the signal goes off once the turn is complete.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-R03","sec04-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check your signal timing","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F09","sec04-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"When on, and when off?","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F09","sec04-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: how far ahead of a turn should your signal be on, and when does it go off? Make your choice, then compare. The answer is at least one hundred feet before the turn, kept on until you actually turn, and switched off once the turn is complete. Signaling at the last moment gives pedestrians and drivers no warning, and leaving it blinking afterward can fool them into thinking you are turning again. If you missed it, remember the order: plan early, signal at one hundred feet, turn, then cancel. That order never changes.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F09","sec04-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Turning recap","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Plan early; signal one hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Right from right; left from inside.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, plan every turn early and move into the proper turn lane well before it once the change is safe. Signal at least one hundred feet ahead, keep the signal on until you turn, and cancel it when the turn is complete. Slow down, check front, rear and sides, keep both hands on the wheel, and give pedestrians the right of way. In daylight you may add hand and arm signals to your lights. On a four-lane or divided highway, turn right from the right lane tightly into the right lane, and turn left from the inside lane without a wide swing, entering just right of the center line.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14","sec04-R01","sec04-R02","sec04-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u03","module_id":"sec04-m03","objective_ids":["sec04-u03"],"title":{"text":"Three-point turns and curves","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F16","sec04-F17"]},"why_how":[{"text":"A three-point turn blocks the road for a moment, so knowing where it is banned keeps you out of the path of traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F16"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Casey misses a street on a two-lane road just below the top of a hill and wants to turn around.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-R04"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Drivers coming over the hill within five hundred feet could not see Casey, and three-point turns are banned there even without a sign.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-R04","sec04-F17"]},"result":{"text":"Casey keeps going and turns around later at a spot visible from far away where traffic makes it safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a three-point turn is legal anywhere no sign forbids it.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04","sec04-F17"]},"correction":{"text":"Local ordinances govern these turns, there may be no warning signs, and they are banned wherever approaching drivers within five hundred feet cannot see you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F17","sec04-R04","sec04-F16"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Seen from far, safe to turn; blind spot, no turn.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-R04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Where are three-point turns banned by the manual?","fact_ids":["sec04-F16"]},"answer":{"text":"On interstate freeways, on curves, and near hilltops where drivers within five hundred feet cannot see you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16"]},"rationale":{"text":"Those places hide you from approaching drivers or carry fast traffic, so turning there would endanger others.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-F15"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Turning around safely","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F16","sec04-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Three-point turns and their limits.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F16","sec04-F18"]},{"text":"Slowing for curves.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F16","sec04-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"Sometimes you need to reverse direction on a street, and the three-point turn is the tool for it. But because the turn briefly blocks the road, the manual sets strict limits on where you may make one. In this lesson you will learn when a three-point turn is normally allowed, the places where it is banned, and why you cannot count on a sign to warn you. We will finish with a related skill, handling curves, because curves are one of the places where turning around is forbidden and where speed control matters most. Let us begin.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F16","sec04-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When a three-point turn fits","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"It must not endanger other traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F17"]},{"text":"You must be visible from far away.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"A three-point turn reverses your direction, and it must not endanger other traffic. For that reason it is normally allowed only where you can be seen from far away and where traffic conditions make it safe. Think about what other drivers need: enough distance to see you blocking part of the road and enough time to slow down. If either is missing, the turn is not safe. Local ordinances govern three-point turns, so the rules can vary by place, and you may find no warning signs at all. If you are unsure whether drivers can see you from far enough away, choose another place to turn around.","fact_ids":["sec04-F15","sec04-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Where the turn is banned","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-F17","sec04-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Interstate freeways and curves.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-F17","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"Hilltops hidden within five hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-F17","sec04-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Three-point turns are banned on interstate freeways, on curves, and near hilltops where drivers approaching within five hundred feet from either direction cannot see you. Each of these places either carries fast traffic or hides you from oncoming drivers until it is too late. Signs that prohibit the turn are usually posted only at especially hazardous spots, so the absence of a sign does not make a turn legal. The visibility rule is the one to carry in your head: if approaching drivers within five hundred feet cannot see you, do not turn.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-F17","sec04-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"No sign is not permission","fact_ids":["sec04-R04","sec04-F17","sec04-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signs may be missing.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04","sec04-F17","sec04-F16"]},{"text":"The visibility limit still applies.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04","sec04-F17","sec04-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many drivers assume that if no sign forbids a three-point turn, it must be allowed. The manual says otherwise. Three-point turns are prohibited where oncoming drivers within five hundred feet cannot see you, even when no sign forbids the turn. Local ordinances govern these turns, warning signs may be absent, and prohibiting signs are usually posted only at the most hazardous spots. So judge the location yourself. Near a curve or a hilltop with poor sight lines, keep going and turn around somewhere visible from far away.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04","sec04-F17","sec04-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the banned places","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Name the three banned places.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: where are three-point turns banned? Picture the answer before you hear it. The answer is on interstate freeways, on curves, and near hilltops where drivers approaching within five hundred feet from either direction cannot see you. Those places either carry fast traffic or hide you from oncoming drivers. Remember too that a sign may not be posted, so the ban applies by the conditions, not by the sign. The safe alternative is to drive on until you reach a spot where you can be seen from far away.","fact_ids":["sec04-F16","sec04-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Taking curves","fact_ids":["sec04-F18","sec04-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slow down before the curve.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18","sec04-F16"]},{"text":"Accelerate slightly while rounding it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F18","sec04-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Curves call for planning, just like turns. Slow down before you reach the curve, so that you do not cross the center line or run off the road. Enter it slowly enough that you can accelerate slightly while rounding the curve, which keeps the car steady. Braking hard in the middle of a curve is what you want to avoid, which is why the slowing happens before it.
